newsitem.title: UK: Triple therapy cuts AIDS deaths, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Triple therapy cuts AIDS deaths, study finds.

text.p: A team of international researchers said on Friday they had proved, in the largest trial ever of its kind, that a triple combination of drugs can help HIV-infected people live longer.
Their trial of 3,500 people in 22 countries showed that starting patients out right away on a triple combination greatly reduced progression to full-blown AIDS and death.
Adding a protease inhibitor to a dual combination of the AIDS cornerstone drug AZT and a similar drug prolonged survival by 50 percent, the study found.

"This is the first study to demonstrate the value of adding a protease inhibitor, such as Invirase (Hoffmann-La Roche's saquinavir) into a standard double nucleoside analogue regimen in previously untreated patients," said Dr Graham Moyle of London's Chelsea and Westminster Hospital.
"This study shows the dramatic benefit of combining saquinavir with ddC (Roche's Hivid) and AZT (Glaxo-Wellcome's -Retrovir) -- a 50 percent reduction in the onset of AIDS."
On Thursday the U.S. Panel on Clinical Practices for Treatment of HIV Infection recommended three-drug therapy as the standard.
Dr Hans Jurgen Stellbrink or University Hospital Eppendorf in Hamburg, Germany, noted that doctors nonetheless "saved" protease inhibitors for when patients had advanced disease.

He said the three-year study showed there was no reason to wait. "It shows that if you take the next step and include a protease inhibitor in the combination it prolongs life and delays progression and death," he said in a telephone interview.

This was probably due to the effects the drug had on the virus. Smaller studies have shown clearly that the triple cocktail can knock the virus down to undetectable levels on both the blood and the lymph glands.
"We saw quite a considerable reduction in viral load," Stellbrink said.
Viral load, or the amount of virus in the blood, is an important indicator of how advanced the HIV infection is.
Stellbrink said his group, which studied volunteers on every continent, would publish their results in a medical journal but felt it important to announce their results straight away.
In the study, sponsored by Roche, volunteers were given either AZT alone, AZT plus ddC, AZT plus ddC plus saquinavir, or saquinavir plus AZT.
"All drugs employed have been relatively well tolerated," Stellbrink said. "Saquinavir is an extremely well-tolerated drug with few side-efects."
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has said protease inhibitors may contribute to diabetes, although it does not recommend that patients stop taking them.

About 150,000 Americans take one of the four approved protease drugs -- Merck & Co's Crixivan (indinavir), Roche's saquinavir, Abbott Laboratories' Norvir (ritonavir) and Agouron Pharmaceuticals' Viracept (nelfinavir).
But the drugs are very expensive -- costing up to $6,000 a year for a protease inhibitor and $3,000 a year each for nucleoside analogues.
